title: Reverse Engineering
description: The reverse engineering exclusion bars R&D credit claims for reproducing an existing component from examination, plans or public information.
summary: The reverse engineering exclusion bars U.S. taxpayers from claiming the federal R&D tax credit under IRC Section 41 for costs of reproducing an existing business component from physical examination, plans, blueprints, detailed specifications, or public information. However, examining a competitor's product while developing the taxpayer's own distinct or improved component does not disqualify later experimental research.

body.text: The reverse engineering exclusion bars U.S. taxpayers from claiming the federal R&D tax credit under IRC Section 41 for costs of reproducing an existing business component from physical examination, plans, blueprints, detailed specifications, or public information. However, examining a competitor's product while developing the taxpayer's own distinct or improved component does not disqualify later experimental research.

Reverse engineering—disassembling, decompiling, or inspecting an existing physical artifact or software system to deduce its design, composition, or operating logic—is categorically excluded from the federal Research and Development (R&D) Tax Credit under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41 when conducted to reproduce an existing business component in whole or in part. Implemented through 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(C) and Treasury Regulation (26 CFR) § 1.41-4(c)(4) as the exclusion for the duplication of an existing business component, federal tax law draws a sharp boundary between uncovering how an existing product already works and resolving genuine technological uncertainty through a systematic process of experimentation. Yet the exclusion does not taint every engineering project that begins by inspecting a competitor's product or a legacy interface: under the express second sentence of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(4), examining an existing business component in the course of developing the taxpayer's own distinct or improved business component does not by itself disqualify subsequent experimental development. Where initial examination ends and independent, hypothesis-driven experimentation begins—isolated where necessary through the shrinking-back rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) or separate production-process evaluation under IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(2)(iii)—the post-examination research expenses remain eligible for the Section 41 credit when substantiated at the discrete business-component level.
Legislative Evolution and Economic Rationale of the Duplication Bar

Congress originally enacted the federal research tax credit as IRC § 44F in Section 221(a) of the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 (Pub. L. No. 97-34, 95 Stat. 172, 241, enacted August 13, 1981, originally applicable to amounts paid or incurred after June 30, 1981) to stimulate domestic research investment, increase capital formation, and enhance economic productivity. Under the original 1981 enactment, IRC § 44F(d) defined "qualified research" simply by cross-reference to the broad meaning of "research or experimental" under IRC § 174, subject only to three exclusions for research conducted outside the United States, research in the social sciences or humanities, and funded research. Following redesignation of § 44F as IRC § 30 by the Deficit Reduction Act of 1984 (July 18, 1984, 98 Stat. 826), Congress grew concerned that taxpayers were interpreting the credit overly broadly to claim virtually any routine product development expense or post-design engineering modification. Through Section 231(b) of the Tax Reform Act of 1986 (Pub. L. No. 99-514, 100 Stat. 2085, 2173), Congress redesignated the provision as IRC § 41 and enacted the restrictive statutory definition of "qualified research" in IRC § 41(d), establishing both the affirmative four-part eligibility test in IRC § 41(d)(1) and the eight categorical exclusions of IRC § 41(d)(4), including the duplication bar in IRC § 41(d)(4)(C).
Correction of the New to the World Versus New to the Taxpayer Chronology

Primary legislative and regulatory authorities demonstrate the opposite sequence prior to 2004. Rather than softening eligibility, the 1986 Act tightened the statute by replacing the simple Section 174 cross-reference with the requirement in IRC § 41(d)(1)(B) that research be undertaken "for the purpose of discovering information" that is technological in nature, alongside the process-of-experimentation requirement in IRC § 41(d)(1)(C). Relying on that 1986 statutory text and following proposed regulations issued on December 2, 1998 (REG-105170-97, 63 FR 66503), final regulations promulgated on January 3, 2001, in Treasury Decision (T.D.) 8930 (66 FR 280, 289–290; also noted in CFR authority tables as 65 FR 287) required taxpayers to seek information that exceeded, expanded, or refined the "common knowledge of skilled professionals in the particular field of science or engineering"—the strict "discovery test".

Following immediate taxpayer objections, the Treasury Department and IRS published Notice 2001-19 (2001-10 I.R.B. 784) on January 31, 2001, announcing an administrative review of T.D. 8930, and issued new proposed regulations on December 26, 2001 (REG-112991-01, 66 FR 66362). On January 2, 2004, the Treasury Department and IRS promulgated final regulations in T.D. 9104 (69 FR 26, RIN 1545-AY82), effective January 2, 2004, and applicable to taxable years ending on or after December 31, 2003 (while also confirming that the IRS would not challenge consistent return positions for taxable years ending before December 31, 2003). Codified at 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i)–(ii), T.D. 9104 eliminated both the T.D. 8930 requirement to advance the common knowledge of skilled professionals and the 2001 proposed regulations' "readily discernible and applicable" phrasing, establishing instead that technical uncertainty is evaluated relative to "the information available to the taxpayer".

When Competitor Y already manufactures and sells a technologically advanced product, its internal architecture, material composition, or algorithmic logic is known to Competitor Y; if Taxpayer X lacks access to Competitor Y's proprietary engineering drawings or source code, that internal design is initially unknown to Taxpayer X. The categorical exclusion of reverse engineering under IRC § 41(d)(4)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(4) resolves this tension by distinguishing genuine experimental discovery from extracting an already-embodied design.
Economic Spillovers, Lead-Time, and the Tax Distinction Between Discovery and Extraction

Samuelson and Scotchmer explain that under intellectual property and trade secret law, permitting reverse engineering in traditional manufacturing industries is economically sound for three reasons: (1) much of the manufacturing know-how remains hidden inside the innovator's factory rather than obvious on the marketed product; (2) physical disassembly, teardown, and re-engineering are inherently costly and time-consuming, preserving a market lead-time window that functions like a de facto short-lived intellectual property right enabling the original innovator to recoup initial R&D investments; and (3) high teardown costs frequently induce second comers to license know-how from the innovator while promoting cumulative knowledge spillovers, interoperability, and price competition. Conversely, Samuelson and Scotchmer demonstrate that market-destructive "free-riding" arises when reverse engineering becomes cheap, rapid, and effortless—such as plug-molding boat hulls or decompiling "information-rich" digital artifacts (computer software, semiconductor chip layouts) that bear their applied know-how on or near the face of the distributed product—collapsing the innovator's lead-time toward zero and preventing R&D recoupment, or when post-reverse-engineering conduct consists solely of deploying competing clones in the market.

Permitting an engineering practice as lawful under trade secret or copyright law does not obligate the public fisc to subsidize it under the Internal Revenue Code. Section 41 is a targeted fiscal incentive designed to subsidize the technical and financial risk of generating new or improved functionality, performance, reliability, or quality when available knowledge does not supply the capability, method, or appropriate design. When a taxpayer physically holds the competitor's finished artifact, blueprint, detailed specification, or binary code, the engineering solution already exists in tangible or machine-readable form. Dissecting that artifact consumes existing spillover know-how to overcome an information asymmetry rather than resolving objective technical uncertainty through scientific experimentation. Consequently, Congress barred reproduction costs under IRC § 41(d)(4)(C) to prevent tax-subsidized free-riding on rival R&D, while preserving credit eligibility under the second sentence of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(4) for post-examination experimental advances that genuinely expand technical capability or design.
Statutory Architecture: The Section 41(d) Four-Part Test and Reverse Engineering

Before reaching the categorical exclusions in IRC § 41(d)(4), a taxpayer bears the affirmative burden of establishing that claimed research activities satisfy all four tests of IRC § 41(d)(1), applied separately to each discrete business component under IRC § 41(d)(2)(A) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(1). Pure reverse engineering routinely fails multiple elements of this four-part gatekeeper framework even before the duplication exclusion of IRC § 41(d)(4)(C) is applied.
1. The Section 174A Domestic R&E Expenditure Test (IRC Section 41(d)(1)(A))

While that cross-reference governed historical tax years (first as "expenses under section 174" prior to 2022, and then as "specified research or experimental expenditures under section 174" for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025, under Pub. L. No. 115-97, § 13206(d)(1)), Public Law 119-21 (Title VII, § 70302, 139 Stat. 72, 190, enacted July 4, 2025, commonly known as the One, Big, Beautiful Bill Act) added IRC § 174A (Domestic research or experimental expenditures) and amended 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) effective for amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. Under current law in 2026, IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) defines qualified research first as research "with respect to which expenditures are treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under section 174A".

Substantively, Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1) (T.D. 6500, 25 FR 11402, Nov. 26, 1960, as amended by T.D. 8562, 59 FR 50160, Oct. 3, 1994, and T.D. 9680, 79 FR 42195, July 21, 2014, generally effective in amended form for taxable years ending on or after July 21, 2014) defines research or experimental expenditures as costs incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business that represent research and development costs in the "experimental or laboratory sense". Expenditures satisfy this definition only if they are for "activities intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product," where "[u]ncertainty exists if the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the product or the appropriate design of the product". Furthermore, 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(5) establishes a component-level rule under which the presence of uncertainty regarding one component of a product does not automatically establish uncertainty across other components or the product as a whole.

In addition, 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(6)(i)–(vii) and the IRS Audit Techniques Guide: Credit for Increasing Research Activities (IRC § 41) — Qualified Research Activities (IRS ATG; administrative guidance last updated June 2005 and subordinate in legal authority to statutes and Treasury regulations) expressly disallow expenditures for (i) ordinary testing or inspection of materials or products for quality control, (ii) efficiency surveys, (iii) management studies, (iv) consumer surveys, (v) advertising or promotions, (vi) the acquisition of another's patent, model, production, or process, or (vii) research in connection with literary, historical, or similar projects. Pure competitive intelligence teardowns conducted merely to catalog how a rival's product is constructed or to acquire another's model or process—without technical uncertainty tied to developing or improving the taxpayer's own product—fail this threshold requirement at the outset.
2. The Discovering Technological Information Test (IRC Section 41(d)(1)(B)(i))

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(i) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)–(4), research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is "technological in nature," meaning the evaluative process must fundamentally rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. As confirmed by T.D. 9104 and the IRS ATG, there is no "discovery" requirement separate and apart from the uncertainty standard of 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1), and the taxpayer need not seek knowledge that exceeds or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the field. Under the regulatory patent safe harbor in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii), issuance of a utility patent under 35 U.S.C. § 151 (other than a design patent under 35 U.S.C. § 171) serves as conclusive evidence that the taxpayer discovered technological information intended to eliminate uncertainty, although obtaining a patent is not a precondition for credit eligibility.

Analysis: Reverse engineering frequently employs advanced scientific instruments and technical tooling—such as coordinate-measuring machines (CMMs), 3D laser scanners, scanning electron microscopes, mass or infrared spectroscopy, integrated-circuit delayering equipment, or software disassemblers and decompilers. However, operating scientific instrumentation merely to observe, measure, and record an existing artifact's physical dimensions, chemical proportions, or compiled object code does not equate to relying on engineering or computer science principles to resolve design uncertainty within an evaluative experiment. As 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(4) confirms, employing computers, laboratory instrumentation, or information technology simply to collect, translate, manipulate, or process data does not by itself establish qualified research.
3. The Business Component Test (IRC Section 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and 26 CFR Section 1.41-4(b)(2))

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and § 41(d)(2)(A)–(B), the taxpayer must intend that the application of the discovered information be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer, and the four-part test must be applied separately to each discrete business component.

Verbatim statutory text in 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(B)(i)–(ii), verbatim regulatory text in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2), and the IRS ATG confirm that a discrete business component is any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be (i) held for sale, lease, or license, or (ii) "used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer". Furthermore, IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) sets forth a mandatory special rule for production processes: "Any plant process, machinery, or technique for commercial production of a business component shall be treated as a separate business component (and not as part of the business component being produced)". Restoring the omitted trade-or-business clause of IRC § 41(d)(2)(B)(ii) and the separate production-process rule of IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) is essential in reverse-engineering controversies because internal manufacturing processes, production lines, and plant techniques used in the taxpayer's trade or business constitute independent business components even when the commercial product being manufactured is an unpatented copy.
4. The Process of Experimentation and 80% Substantially All Rule (IRC Section 41(d)(1)(C))

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and § 41(d)(3)(A)–(B), "substantially all" of the research activities with respect to a business component must constitute elements of a process of experimentation relating to a qualified purpose—defined in IRC § 41(d)(3)(A) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii) as a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality of the business component, while IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) expressly disqualifies activities relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors. Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) requires a process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where capability, method, or appropriate design is uncertain at the outset, encompassing three sequential elements:

items: Identification of uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component (where capability, method, or appropriate design is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities);
Identification of one or more alternatives intended to eliminate that uncertainty; and

Identification and conduct of a process of evaluating those alternatives—such as modeling, simulation, or a systematic trial-and-error methodology relying on principles of the hard sciences, engineering, or computer science.

body.text: Crucially, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) cautions that uncertainty regarding appropriate design at the outset "does not establish that all activities undertaken to achieve that new or improved business component constitute a process of experimentation," and the IRS ATG stresses that merely demonstrating that uncertainty was eliminated is insufficient. Pure reverse engineering proceeds linearly from disassembly to observation to documentation. Rather than formulating competing hypotheses and systematically evaluating design alternatives, the engineer extracts the pre-existing solution already embedded in the rival's product.

Furthermore, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) defines "substantially all" quantitatively: 80 percent or more of a taxpayer's research activities with respect to a business component, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis (and without regard to 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2)), must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose. Equally significant is the explicit proviso in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6): when the 80% threshold is met, the remaining 20% (or less) of research activities on that component qualify only "so long as these remaining research activities satisfy the requirements of section 41(d)(1)(A) and are not otherwise excluded under section 41(d)(4)". Excluded duplication activities under IRC § 41(d)(4)(C) can therefore never be swept into eligible Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) inside the remaining 20% non-experimental allowance.
5. Categorical Statutory Exclusions Under IRC Section 41(d)(4)

Regardless of whether a taxpayer argues that a project touches upon product engineering, the flush language of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1), 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(A)–(H), and the IRS Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. Dec. 2025) disallow eight excluded activity categories from the definition of qualified research:

items: Research after commercial production (IRC § 41(d)(4)(A) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(2)): Any research conducted after the beginning of commercial production of the business component (including preproduction planning, tooling-up for production, trial production runs, and troubleshooting production equipment);

Adaptation of existing business components (IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(3)): Any research related to adapting an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need;

Duplication of existing business component (IRC § 41(d)(4)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(4)): Any research related to reproducing an existing business component (in whole or in part) from a physical examination of the business component itself or from plans, blueprints, detailed specifications, or publicly available information with respect to such business component;

Surveys, studies, etc. (IRC § 41(d)(4)(D) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(5)): Any (i) efficiency survey, (ii) activity relating to management function or technique, (iii) market research, testing, or development (including advertising or promotions), (iv) routine data collection, or (v) routine or ordinary testing or inspection for quality control;

Computer software for internal use (IRC § 41(d)(4)(E) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)): Except as provided in regulations, research with respect to internal-use computer software other than software for use in an activity constituting qualified research or a qualifying production process;
Foreign research (IRC § 41(d)(4)(F) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(7)): Any research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any possession of the United States;
Social sciences, etc. (IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(8)): Any research in the social sciences, arts, or humanities; and
Funded research (IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(9)): Any research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or governmental entity.

body.text: Deconstructing the Duplication Exclusion: IRC Section 41(d)(4)(C) and Regulation Section 1.41-4(c)(4)

Enacted in the Tax Reform Act of 1986, 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(C) excludes from qualified research "[a]ny research related to the reproduction of an existing business component (in whole or in part) from a physical examination of the business component itself or from plans, blueprints, detailed specifications, or publicly available information with respect to such business component". Implementing this statutory exclusion for taxable years ending on or after December 31, 2003, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(4) states verbatim:

"(4) Duplication of existing business component. Activities relating to reproducing an existing business component (in whole or in part) from a physical examination of the business component itself or from plans, blueprints, detailed specifications, or publicly available information about the business component are not qualified research. This exclusion does not apply merely because the taxpayer examines an existing business component in the course of developing its own business component."

The operational reach of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(4) turns on three textual features. First, the parenthetical phrase "(in whole or in part)" prevents taxpayers from sheltering partial reverse engineering inside a broader new product development effort. If an industrial equipment manufacturer develops a genuinely novel machine overall, yet disassembles and copies a competitor's fuel pump, circuit board, or mechanical valve to replicate that sub-assembly inside its new machine, all activities relating to reproducing that sub-assembly are excluded in part. Second, because the regulation bars "[a]ctivities relating to reproducing," ancillary technical work integral to copying—configuring teardown fixtures, running chemical spectrum assays to mirror an unpatented formula, converting CMM or laser-scan point clouds into computer-aided design (CAD) models, delayering semiconductor dies to copy layout masks, or decompiling binaries to replicate source logic—falls within the disqualified scope.

Excluded as to all inspection and reproduction work; subsequent independent design work qualifies only if examination fails to resolve capability, method, or design uncertainty.
Building or coding a component from licensed, acquired, or archived schematics, CAD drawings, or architectural plans.
Excluded; original plans eliminate design uncertainty, rendering fabrication routine engineering or production.
Reproducing an existing component from detailed design specifications or vendor reference designs that prescribe how to build the component.
Excluded when specifications dictate the internal design solution; distinguished from high-level functional or performance targets where internal design or method remains uncertain.
Reproducing an existing component from published patents, technical literature, industry standards, or public open-source code repositories.
Excluded for copying or porting existing code or patented embodiments; permitted when public literature is consulted as background before experimenting on unresolved technical problems.
IRC § 41(d)(4)(D); 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(6); IRS ATG; Form 6765 Instructions
Measuring a competitor product's external performance metrics without dissecting internal mechanisms (surveys, studies, routine data collection, or quality/efficiency testing).
Excluded as non-experimental studies or routine data collection; however, benchmark metrics may define the target performance improvement for a subsequent qualified experimentation project.

body.text: Benchmarking Distinguished From Reverse Engineering

Competitive benchmarking and reverse engineering both examine rival products, yet they fail under distinct statutory provisions. Competitive benchmarking measures external performance outputs—such as cycle speed, structural load capacity, power consumption, or high-temperature failure thresholds—without dissecting the internal mechanism, falling outside qualified research as efficiency surveys, routine data collection, or ordinary testing and inspection under IRC § 41(d)(4)(D)(i), (iv), and (v) and 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(6)(i)–(ii). Reverse engineering dissects the physical or digital artifact to uncover how the rival achieved that performance, triggering IRC § 41(d)(4)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(4) when used to reproduce the mechanism in whole or in part.
Accurately stated under federal tax jurisprudence, excluded reverse engineering is observational and extractive of an existing design rather than investigative of an unresolved technical unknown.
Regulatory Boundary Lines: Correcting the Example 8 Paradigm

Treasury Regulations illustrate the operation of the IRC § 41(d)(4) exclusions in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10), noting in the introductory text that the examples illustrate paragraphs (c)(1) through (c)(9) (excepting paragraph (c)(6) on internal-use software) and carry no automatic inference regarding satisfaction of IRC § 41(d)(1) unless explicitly stated. Both the IRS Software Audit Guidelines and tax practitioners rely on 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 8 as the central regulatory illustration of the duplication exclusion.

First, the fine-shred food product and breaking shredding-blade scenario actually resides in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(8), Example 3, which illustrates the affirmative Process of Experimentation and 80% "substantially all" rules under § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6) rather than the duplication exclusion. In 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(8), Example 3:

"X is engaged in the business of manufacturing food products and currently manufactures a large-shred version of a product. X seeks to modify its current production line to permit it to manufacture both a large-shred version and a fine-shred version of one of its food products. A smaller, thinner shredding blade capable of producing a fine-shred version of the food product, however, is not commercially available. Thus, X must develop a new shredding blade that can be fitted onto its current production line. X is uncertain concerning the design of the new shredding blade, because the material used in its existing blade breaks when machined into smaller, thinner blades. X engages in a systematic trial and error process of analyzing various blade designs and materials to determine whether the new shredding blade must be constructed of a different material from that of its existing shredding blade and, if so, what material will best meet X's functional requirements."

As 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(8), Example 3(ii) concludes, Taxpayer X's activities to develop the new shredding blade satisfy the process-of-experimentation requirement without examining or copying any competitor's product.

Second, actual 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 8 addresses a competitor's three-ingredient gasoline additive. In actual Example 8(i), Competitor Y manufactures an existing gasoline additive using three ingredients: A, B, and C. Taxpayer X seeks to develop and manufacture its own gasoline additive that "appears and functions in a manner similar to Y's additive". X analyzes Y's additive and reproduces ingredients A and B, with only insignificant differences immaterial to viability, effectiveness, or cost. However, X wishes to combine A and B with a third ingredient having a materially lower cost than ingredient C, and X therefore conducts a process of experimentation to develop, analyze, and test potential alternative formulations of the additive.
The Regulatory Holding of Actual Example 8 and the Post-Examination Pivot
The verbatim regulatory conclusion in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 8(ii) splits Taxpayer X's project cleanly along the boundary between reproduction and experimentation:

"X's activities in analyzing and reproducing ingredients A and B involve duplication of existing business components and are excluded from the definition of qualified research under section 41(d)(4)(C) and paragraph (c)(4) of this section. X's experimentation activities to develop potential alternative formulations of the additive do not involve duplication of an existing business component and are not excluded from the definition of qualified research under section 41(d)(4)(C) and paragraph (c)(4) of this section."

Actual Example 8 establishes that partial reverse engineering does not poison subsequent independent formulation or design research, even when the taxpayer explicitly aims to sell a competing product that functions similarly to the competitor's offering and directly copies two of its three ingredients. Whenever competitive examination reveals that complete replication is economically or technically unviable—whether because an ingredient is prohibitively expensive (as with ingredient C in Example 8), blocked by active utility patents, incompatible with existing plant tooling, or dependent on unidentifiable metallurgy or proprietary firmware—the project pivots out of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(4) duplication. From that pivot forward, the appropriate design, material, or formulation must be discovered by evaluating alternatives under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5), while all labor and supply costs expended on analyzing and reproducing the copied components (ingredients A and B) remain strictly excluded.
Software Reverse Engineering, Interoperability, and Clean Room Development

Software engineering creates heightened audit friction under IRC § 41(d)(4)(C) because compiled binaries, database tables, and protocol streams carry applied logic directly inside distributed digital artifacts. While administrative audit guidelines carry less legal weight than the Internal Revenue Code or Treasury Regulations, they govern how IRS examiners classify and challenge software claims in practice.
IRS High Risk Classification and Embedded Software Workflows

To focus examination resources on software activities at the greatest risk of failing IRC § 41(d), the IRS Software Audit Guidelines rank software development tasks across three qualitative categories—"low risk," "moderate risk," and "high risk"—explicitly defining "high risk" to mean that such activities "usually fail to constitute qualified research under I.R.C. § 41(d)". Specifically, the IRS Software Audit Guidelines enumerate eight high-risk software categories: (1) modifying software to use new devices or standards; (2) developing a business component that is substantially similar in technology, functionality, and features to capabilities already in existence at other companies; (3) upgrading to newer versions of hardware or software, or installing vendor fix releases; (4) re-hosting or porting an application to new hardware; (5) interface software development; (6) Y2K program changes; (7) vendor product extensions; and (8) graphical user interfaces (GUIs).

Reverse engineering is placed squarely in the high-risk category. The guidelines explain that software reverse engineering typically consists of examining existing programs, databases, and files to figure out how an existing application really works, and state flatly that reverse engineering is not qualified research under IRC § 41(d), citing Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 8. As the IRS Software Audit Guidelines emphasize, activities involving reverse engineering are generally not directed at resolving software development uncertainties through identifying and conducting a process designed to evaluate alternatives based on principles of computer science, but are instead directed at verifying compatibility, defining interface requirements, or ensuring software operates according to vendor or device standards.

Beyond standalone decompilation of rival products, the IRS Software Audit Guidelines alert examiners that excluded reverse engineering frequently occurs embedded within four common software engineering workflows:

items: Software Maintenance: Referencing the IEEE Standard for Software Maintenance (Software Engineering Standards Committee of the IEEE Computer Society, June 25, 1998, pp. 3–4), the guidelines note that corrective, adaptive, and perfective maintenance routinely combine code analysis, debugging, and reverse engineering prior to modifying existing programs.

Device and Standards Modification: Modifying existing software to support new or existing standards or devices typically relies on code and documentation inspection, reverse engineering, debugging, and routine testing to pinpoint insertion points where code changes must be made.

Vendor Compliance Testing: Running a target vendor's validation or certification test suite, reviewing test results, and resolving failures through debugging and reverse engineering fail the process-of-experimentation test because they verify compliance with another vendor's standard rather than resolving underlying computer-science uncertainty.

Vendor Product Extensions: Writing customer code to fill functional gaps in existing vendor software (such as custom report formatting or calculations) using vendor-provided Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) or user exits without modifying core vendor software is treated as routine implementation rather than experimental computer science.

body.text: Interoperability, Legacy Interfaces, and API Bridges

Software teams often reverse engineer undocumented file formats, legacy databases, or proprietary communication protocols not to clone a target program, but to achieve application-to-application or business-to-business interoperability. Addressing legacy integration and interface software development directly, the IRS Software Audit Guidelines note that defining data and transaction requirements on both ends of an interface (whether internal application-to-application, external business-to-business, or adding a web browser interface to a PC application) frequently requires engineers to reverse engineer the data interface supported by an existing legacy application—and that legacy interface reverse engineering is disqualified under IRC § 41(d).

Analysis: Although the IRS Software Audit Guidelines do not address post-examination interoperability coding beyond disqualifying the interface definition and reverse-engineering work itself, reading the second sentence of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(4) alongside 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5) establishes a disciplined two-phase boundary. All engineering hours spent inspecting packet captures, hex dumps, legacy database schemas, or compiled binaries to map how an external system formats or exchanges data must be excluded as reverse engineering and routine data collection under IRC § 41(d)(4)(C) and (D)(iv). Once those external interface requirements are mapped, however, developing the taxpayer's own new translation engine, real-time API bridge, or high-throughput cryptographic pipeline can qualify as a separate software subcomponent if achieving required throughput, stream latency, memory efficiency, or fault tolerance across incompatible architectures remains technologically uncertain and demands systematic evaluation of competing algorithmic designs—whereas routine field-to-field data mapping and protocol formatting involve no design uncertainty and fail 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5).
Clean Room Software Development and the Detailed Specifications Trap

To guard against copyright infringement when building compatible software or firmware, technology companies frequently utilize a two-team "Clean Room" architecture: Team A ("Dirty Room") disassembles or decompiles the existing binary and drafts a specification, while Team B ("Clean Room")—isolated by strict access controls from ever viewing the target code—writes new source code to satisfy that specification.

The IRS Software Audit Guidelines contain no mention of clean-room development and confer no automatic tax safe harbor on Clean Room Team B. Consequently, if Team A hands Team B detailed internal design specifications—prescribing state machines, data structures, memory layouts, or step-by-step algorithms extracted from the target program—Team B's coding will still be disallowed as reproduction from "detailed specifications" under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(4) and for lack of design uncertainty under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5), despite complete copyright cleanliness. Team B's engineering hours qualify only when Team A's handoff is restricted to high-level functional or black-box input/output requirements (and error conditions), leaving the internal software architecture and algorithmic methods genuinely uncertain so that Team B must independently hypothesize, model, and test competing implementation alternatives.
Judicial Precedent Governing Uncertainty, Verification, and Activity Thresholds
Four federal tax decisions police the boundary between existing market functionality, routine verification calculations, systematic experimentation, and the 80% "substantially all" threshold.
1. Union Carbide Corp. and Subsidiaries v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50, aff'd, 697 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. 2012)

Furthermore, Union Carbide and the Second Circuit's affirmance demonstrate that raw materials or supplies used in commercial production runs for sale do not become qualified research supplies merely because plant process tests are conducted during manufacture. Applied to reverse engineering, ad-hoc probing of circuit traces, chemical compounds, or encrypted files merely to observe how an existing system behaves lacks hypothesis-driven evaluation of design alternatives under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i).
2. Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201 (2014)

Official IRS Chief Counsel Advice, Internal Revenue Bulletin citations, and state administrative rulings confirm the sole correct caption is Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201, 108 T.C.M. (CCH) 355 (decided October 1, 2014, by Judge Vasquez; consolidated Docket Nos. 14435-09, 14460-09, 6183-10, and 6210-10). As detailed in legal and tax practitioner case summaries of the Tax Court opinion, petitioner Eric G. Suder (CEO and 90% shareholder) and Douglas J. Boyd (President/COO and 10% shareholder) litigated pass-through Section 41 research credits claimed by Subchapter S corporation Estech Systems, Inc. (ESI), a designer and manufacturer of integrated business telephone hardware and software systems, for tax years 2004 through 2007. Having begun in 1987 by testing, repackaging, and reselling liquidated Candela private branch exchanges (PBXs), ESI evolved into an ISO-9000-certified engineering organization of roughly 125 employees (including approximately 40 engineers) developing proprietary PBX hardware and embedded software across 76 claimed projects during 2004–2007, of which the parties stipulated 12 representative projects for trial.

According to these practitioner case analyses and administrative tribunal summaries, the IRS and its expert witness (Dr. Charles Jackson) argued in Suder that ESI's projects were routine engineering or duplications because features such as voicemail, caller ID, automated attendants, and IP telephony already existed in competing commercial phone systems sold by industry giants like Avaya and Cisco, and because ESI engineers consulted publicly available technical standards. Judge Vasquez rejected the IRS's position and held that 11 of the 12 representative projects satisfied all four tests of IRC § 41(d)(1) (while 1 project involving maintenance/bug-fixing of an existing commercial product failed). Because ESI's hardware schematics and software architecture were proprietary, ESI's engineers could not copy competitor designs or download off-the-shelf code; instead, they confronted genuine uncertainty regarding capability, method, and appropriate circuit and firmware design (such as resolving current spikes and noise on the DLC82 project, adapting Linux to proprietary hardware on the Mad Max project, and integrating hardware/software on the IVC1212 project) and resolved those uncertainties through a structured, multi-level process of schematic design, Gerber-file prototype fabrication, oscilloscope/logic-analyzer testing, and alpha/beta testing.

At the same time, practitioner analyses highlight that Suder sounded a major warning on executive wage QREs: on an issue of first impression under IRC § 174(e), the Tax Court held that although 75% of CEO Suder's time constituted qualified services (conceptualizing product features, reviewing specifications, and alpha testing every prototype), a substantial portion of his $8.7 million to $11 million annual compensation was unreasonable relative to his technical services, reducing eligible CEO wage QREs to roughly 20% of the claimed compensation while waiving IRC § 6662(a) penalties for reasonable cause and good-faith reliance on CPA advice under 26 CFR § 1.6664-4(b). For reverse-engineering analysis, Suder illustrates that under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii), developing functional capabilities already present in rival products is credit-eligible when the taxpayer does not copy the competitor's internal implementation but instead resolves platform-specific design uncertainty through independent experimentation ("Neither section 41 nor the regulations thereunder require taxpayers to 'reinvent the wheel'").
3. Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113 (Decided December 23, 2024)

Consistent legal and CPA firm analyses confirm that the case was decided in the U.S. Tax Court on December 23, 2024, under Docket No. 4759-22 as Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113. As reported in those practitioner analyses, Phoenix Design Group, Inc. (PDG), a Tennessee C-corporation operating as a multidisciplinary consulting firm designing mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and fire protection (MEPF) systems for buildings (claiming credits across more than 200 projects for tax years 2013–2016), litigated three sampled projects: Gerald Champion Military Psychiatric Unit (Project No. 13008.00), Baptist Memorial Hospital–North Mississippi Oxford (BHNM Oxford, Project No. 13003.00), and Vanderbilt University Engineering and Science Building (VUESB, Project No. 12010.01).

As summarized across legal and accounting firm reviews of the opinion, the Tax Court disallowed 100% of the claimed research credits and sustained 20% accuracy-related penalties under IRC § 6662 across three core holdings directly relevant to reverse engineering and design verification:

items: Standard Calculations and Available Data Fail Section 174 Uncertainty: The court held that performing standard engineering calculations on available data (such as sizing HVAC ductwork from airflow parameters, calculating laboratory exhaust plume height, or referencing historical data and building codes) is not an investigative Section 174 activity because existing information already establishes the appropriate design. Furthermore, echoing 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(5), the court held that uncertainty concerning a single room or piece of equipment (such as final equipment selection in a hybrid operating room) does not create design uncertainty across the entire building MEPF system. This reinforces why taking physical measurements, verifying dimensions, or running standard load checks on an existing competitor product fails IRC §§ 174A and 41(d)(1)(A).

Linear Design Phases Are Not a Process of Experimentation: PDG's six-stage design workflow (following standard American Institute of Architects (AIA) phases from Pre-Design and Schematic Design through Construction Documents) was linear rather than iterative and hypothesis-driven, and drawings revised to accommodate client preferences (such as moving air-handling units to a roof) lacked documented systematic evaluation of alternatives under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5).

Failure of Unsubstantiated Shrink-Back: The court explained that while a failed overall building-system claim could theoretically shrink back under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) to a discrete engineering subsystem (such as an HVAC or plumbing subcomponent), shrink-back cannot be applied to a chronological "design phase" or to unsegregated employee timesheets that fail to separate qualified from non-qualified work or distinguish engineers from CAD drafters.

body.text: 4. Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. March 7, 2023)

The controlling appellate framework is established in Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287, No. 21-3145 (7th Cir. Mar. 7, 2023) (authored by Circuit Judge Brennan, joined by Circuit Judges Rovner and Hamilton), affirming Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-15 (U.S. Tax Court Docket No. 17431-17). As detailed in the Seventh Circuit opinion and Tax Court case summaries, Corn Island Shipyard, Inc. (CIS), an Indiana shipbuilding subsidiary of Little Sandy Coal, claimed $1,141,713 in Section 41 credits for the taxable year ended June 30, 2014 (resulting in a $324,529 tax deficiency and $64,910 accuracy-related penalty under IRC § 6662) across 11 vessels, tried via representative projects including the Apex 720 tanker barge ("Project 720", modified from an earlier vessel, the Penn 80, with $2,505,491 in claimed production wages, $3,892,142 in supplies, and $17,504 in weld-testing contract expenses) and the Detyens floating dry dock ("Project 730", with $146,109 in claimed wages and $1,943,265 in supplies).

Affirming the disallowance of all credits and accuracy-related penalties, both the Tax Court and the Seventh Circuit rejected the taxpayer's "novelty" and physical-proportion theory (where CIS argued that because 87% to 90% of the Apex 720 hull and physical elements differed from the earlier Penn 80 vessel, the 80% rule was met)—holding that under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), the 80% "substantially all" requirement is measured strictly by research activities (on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis), not by physical elements or whether a vessel as a whole is first-in-class. Notably, the Seventh Circuit corrected the Tax Court on one legal point regarding the fraction's structure: whereas the Tax Court had excluded production employees fabricating pilot models from the numerator as "experimentation by association," the Seventh Circuit held that direct support and direct supervision activities (including pilot-model fabrication wages directly supporting experimental research under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)) belong in both the numerator and the denominator of the 80% fraction rather than solely in the denominator. Even under that corrected fraction, however, CIS lost 100% of its claim because its engineers and managers (such as lead naval architect Bud Johnson, allocated at a flat 60% estimate across $609,276 of unallocated nonproduction wages) kept no project-specific time logs and relied on arbitrary management percentage estimates rather than a principled, non-arbitrary evidentiary accounting showing that at least 80% of activities on either vessel constituted elements of a process of experimentation.

For projects involving reverse engineering, Little Sandy Coal makes subcomponent cost segregation critical: if excluded competitive teardown and reproduction activities exceed 20% of total hours or costs booked to an unsegregated product project, the entire product fails the 80% threshold of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), resulting in 100% disallowance unless contemporaneous records permit shrinking back to a qualifying sub-assembly under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2).
Strategic Remediation: The Shrinking-Back Rule and Separate Production Processes

When an engineering project incorporates competitive teardown analysis or copied components alongside genuine technical innovation, two regulatory rules permit taxpayers to isolate eligible research activities cleanly: the shrinking-back rule for subcomponents (26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2)) and separate evaluation of manufacturing processes (IRC § 41(d)(2)(C), 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2), and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(2)(iii)).
Mechanics of the Shrinking-Back Rule (26 CFR Section 1.41-4(b)(2))
Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2), the eligibility requirements of IRC § 41(d) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a) are applied first at the level of the discrete overall business component:

"(2) Shrinking-back rule. The requirements of section 41(d) and paragraph (a) of this section are to be applied first at the level of the discrete business component, that is, the product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer. If these requirements are not met at that level, then they apply at the most significant subset of elements of the product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license. This shrinking back of the product is to continue until either a subset of elements of the product that satisfies the requirements is reached, or the most basic element of the product is reached and such element fails to satisfy the test. This shrinking-back rule is applied only if a taxpayer does not satisfy the requirements of section 41(d)(1) and paragraph (a)(2) of this section with respect to the overall business component. The shrinking-back rule is not itself applied as a reason to exclude research activities from credit eligibility."

If the overall component fails IRC § 41(d)(1) (for instance, because reverse engineering and reproducing outer housings or ingredients A and B dilute the process-of-experimentation ratio below 80%), the requirements are applied iteratively to the most significant subset of elements until a qualifying subcomponent is reached. Regulation § 1.41-4(b)(2) specifies that the shrinking-back rule applies only when the overall component fails Section 41(d)(1) and is never applied by the IRS as a weapon to exclude otherwise qualifying activities. Consistent with Phoenix Design Group, the shrunk-back unit must be a discrete physical or functional subset of elements (such as a drive-spring sub-assembly, an HVAC subsystem, or a software encryption module), not a chronological project phase, and must be backed by component-specific time and cost records.
Separate Evaluation of Manufacturing Processes (IRC Section 41(d)(2)(C) and 26 CFR Section 1.41-4(c)(2)(iii))

More precisely, 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(C) mandates by statute that "[a]ny plant process, machinery, or technique for commercial production of a business component shall be treated as a separate business component (and not as part of the business component being produced)". Implementing this mandate, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) defines a "process" used in the taxpayer's trade or business as its own discrete business component, and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(2)(iii) confirms that in cases involving development of both a product and a manufacturing or commercial production process for that product, Section 41(d) eligibility applies separately to the product and the production process—"even after a product meets the taxpayer's basic functional and economic requirements, activities relating to the development of the manufacturing process still may constitute qualified research, provided that the development of the process itself separately satisfies the requirements of section 41(d) and this section, and the activities are conducted before the process meets the taxpayer's basic functional and economic requirements or is ready for commercial use".

Consequently, if a domestic manufacturer reverse engineers an unpatented plastic bracket or off-patent pharmaceutical compound to sell an exact generic replacement, 100% of product-design expenses on the bracket or molecule are excluded duplication under IRC § 41(d)(4)(C). Yet if fabricating that bracket or synthesizing that compound within target cycle times, purity levels, or dimensional tolerances requires systematically experimenting with novel injection-molding tooling, multi-cavity thermal cooling channels, or continuous-flow catalytic reactors, the manufacturing process qualifies independently as its own discrete business component under IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(2)(iii).

body.text: Hypothetical Worked Example 1: Medical Injector Teardown and Subcomponent Shrink-Back

Engineers spend 250 hours ($25,000, or 25.0% of total hours) disassembling a rival's commercial injector pen, taking CMM dimensional measurements, and duplicating the outer plastic housing (excluded duplication under IRC § 41(d)(4)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(4)). Discovering that the rival's proprietary drive-spring alloy cannot be sourced or replicated, engineers spend 700 hours ($70,000, or 70.0% of total hours) running finite-element simulations and fatigue-testing three alternative spring alloys and coil geometries to achieve consistent injection force across temperature extremes (process of experimentation under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)). Finally, 50 hours ($5,000, or 5.0% of total hours) are logged to initial activity on the drive-spring subproject—evaluated under two alternative factual variations: in Case A, those 50 hours represent non-evaluative technical scoping for the new alloy that satisfies IRC § 174A / § 41(d)(1)(A) uncertainty and is not excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4); in Case B, those 50 hours represent chemically assaying the rival's original spring in a failed attempt to copy it before pivoting to new alloys (excluded reproduction-related work under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(4)).

items: Step 1 — Overall Injector Pen Evaluation (1,000 Hours / $100,000): Evaluated at the overall product level, 700 of the 1,000 hours (700 / 1,000 = 70.0%) constitute elements of a process of experimentation. Because 70.0% falls short of the 80.0% "substantially all" floor in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), the overall product fails IRC § 41(d)(1)(C), resulting in $0 in eligible QREs if subcomponent hours were not tracked separately.

Step 2 — Shrinking Back to the Drive-Spring Sub-Assembly (750 Hours / $75,000): Segregating and conceding the 250 hours ($25,000) of outer-housing duplication allows the taxpayer to shrink back under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) to the discrete 750-hour ($75,000) Drive-Spring Mechanism. On that subcomponent, the experimentation share rises to 700 / 750 = 93.33% (93.3%), exceeding the 80.0% threshold.

Step 3 — Applying the 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) Remainder Proviso (Case A vs. Case B): Under Case A, because the remaining 50 hours (50 / 750 = 6.67%, or 6.7%) satisfy IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) (§ 174A) and are not excluded under § 41(d)(4), all 750 subcomponent hours qualify under the ≤20% remainder rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), yielding 750 hours × $100/hour = $75,000 in QREs. Under Case B, even though the subcomponent still passes the 80.0% experimentation test (93.33%), the remaining 50 hours ($5,000) are excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(C); under the express proviso of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), excluded § 41(d)(4) hours cannot qualify within the ≤20% remainder and must be carved out, yielding 700 hours × $100/hour = $70,000 in eligible QREs.

body.text: Hypothetical Worked Example 2: Individual Software Engineer Nexus Segregation

Recording a single blended timesheet line (100 hours — Legacy Integration) prevents establishing nexus between wages and qualified activities, exposing all $12,000 to audit disallowance under the IRS ATG, Little Sandy Coal, and Phoenix Design Group. Conversely, booking 20 hours to Phase 1: Legacy Interface Analysis (Non-Qualified) and 80 hours to Phase 2: Translation Module Latency Experimentation (Qualified) isolates the 80-hour module at 100% experimentation (80 / 80 = 100.0%, or 80.0% across the 100 hours with the 20 excluded § 41(d)(4)(C) hours carved out), substantiating $9,600 in wage QREs while excluding $2,400.
Substantiation, Business-Component Nexus, and Form 6765 Section G Reporting

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d) and IRC § 6001 (as clarified in T.D. 9104), taxpayers claiming Section 41 research credits must retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit. The IRS ATG emphasizes that the burden of proof rests on the taxpayer across all elements of IRC § 41(d)(1), requiring a direct nexus linking employee wages, supplies, and contract research expenses to each discrete business component (or shrunk-back subset) rather than grouping all research into one broad category. During examination, IRS examiners issue Information Document Requests (IDRs) demanding a complete list and description of each claimed project or activity tied to its specific business component and conduct technical interviews with engineers to supplement and corroborate contemporaneous written records.
Mandatory Business-Component Disclosure on Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025)

Reinforcing the judicial documentation standards enforced in Little Sandy Coal and Phoenix Design Group, the IRS Instructions for Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities, Rev. Dec. 2025) establish granular upfront reporting in Section G (Business Component Information). While Section G is optional on timely filed original returns for tax years beginning before 2026 (unless filing an amended return), Section G is mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025 unless the filer qualifies for an exemption—specifically, where the taxpayer either (a) is a qualified small business under IRC § 41(h)(3) electing the reduced payroll tax credit, or (b) reports a research credit on an original return while having controlled-group QREs of $1.5 million or less and average annual gross receipts over the prior three tax years (determined under IRC § 448(c)(3)) of $50 million or less.

Under the "80%/Top 50" requirement in the Form 6765 Instructions (Rev. Dec. 2025), non-exempt filers completing Section G must itemize business components in descending order of QREs covering at least 80% of total QREs (reported by each controlled-group member filing a separate return with respect to at least 80% of its own total QREs), capped at no more than 50 business components, and report any remaining components on a single line labeled "Aggregate Business Components" in Column 49(c) (filling in aggregate wage, supply, and contract QREs in Columns 50 through 56 while leaving Columns 49(a), 49(b), 49(d), 49(e), and 49(f) blank). For each itemized business component, Section G requires reporting the Employer Identification Number (EIN) of the entity conducting the research in Column 49(a); the Principal Business Activity (PBA) code of that entity in Column 49(b); and the name or unique alphanumeric identifier of the business component consistent with books and records in Column 49(c) (appending "sample" if statistical sampling under Rev. Proc. 2011-42 is used, along with attaching Form6765StatSamplePlan.pdf, or entering "ASC 730 Directive" if electing the ASC 730 Directive on Line 41). Filers must then designate the business component type in Column 49(d) (1. Product, 2. Process, or 3. All Others encompassing computer software, technique, formula, or invention); specify the software classification where applicable in Column 49(e) (A. IUS—internal use software, B. DFS—dual function software, C. Non-IUS, or D. Excepted from IUS treatment); describe the specific information sought to be discovered in Column 49(f) whenever claiming a new or increased Section 41 credit on an amended return or Administrative Adjustment Request (AAR) (not required on timely filed original returns); and disaggregate in-house wage QREs across actual conduct of qualified research (Column 50), direct supervision / first-line management (Column 51), and direct support (Column 52), followed by supply, computer rental/lease, contract research, and total QREs in Columns 53 through 56.

Analysis: Because Form 6765 Section G requires identifying each qualifying business component (and categorizing it as 1. Product, 2. Process, or 3. All Others) directly on the original tax return for tax years beginning after 2025 (and on all amended refund claims), taxpayers can no longer defer shrink-back analysis until an IRS audit. Whenever competitive teardowns precede subcomponent or manufacturing-process innovation, the shrunk-back subcomponent (26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2)) or separate production process (2. Process under IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(2)(iii)) must be defined and accounted for in the taxpayer's books and records prior to filing the return.

cells: Separate project/task codes dividing Phase 1: Competitive Teardown / Legacy Interface Analysis from Phase 2: Subcomponent Experimental Development, disaggregating direct conduct, direct supervision, and direct support wages (Form 6765 Columns 50–52).
Establishes quantitative nexus; prevents excluded duplication hours from diluting the 80% experimentation fraction under Little Sandy Coal.
Contemporaneous engineering memo documenting why an inspected competitor artifact, ingredient, or reference design failed constraints, used unavailable materials, or could not be copied.
Substantiates technical uncertainty at the start of Phase 2 (26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1)) and invokes the second-sentence exception of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(4).

Satisfies the three-step evaluative mandate of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) and refutes linear-design disallowance under Phoenix Design Group.

Corroborates systematic trial-and-error or modeling methodology rather than routine dimension or code verification.

body.text: Actionable Compliance Protocol for Engineering and Tax Teams
Organizations whose R&D pipelines incorporate competitive teardowns, benchmarking, or legacy software integration should execute five operational steps prior to claiming Section 41 credits:

items: Enforce Phase-Gate Time and Cost Segregation: Configure enterprise resource planning (ERP) and engineering time-tracking systems so physical teardowns, CMM dimensional scanning, chemical spectrum assays, and legacy-interface mapping are recorded under non-creditable cost centers (Phase 1 — Competitive Analysis / Duplication) strictly separated from subsequent experimental subcomponent development (Phase 2 — Subcomponent Experimentation), while tracking actual conduct, direct supervision, and direct support wages separately to populate Form 6765 Section G Columns 50–52.

Record Contemporaneous "Impossibility of Replication" Memos: Require lead engineers to document the exact technical barrier—prohibitive ingredient cost (as in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 8), proprietary material unavailability, utility patent restrictions, plant tooling incompatibility, or thermal/latency failure—that prevented copying an examined product and necessitated independent experimentation.

Define Shrunk-Back Subcomponents Prior to Return Filing: Proactively apply 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) (for physical sub-assemblies or software modules) or IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(2)(iii) (for manufacturing processes) during annual credit preparation so Form 6765 Section G Column 49(c) and Column 49(d) list the precise qualifying subcomponent or process rather than an overinclusive commercial product.

Scrub Software Integration and Clean-Room Specs Against 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(4): Exclude embedded reverse-engineering hours inside software maintenance, device/standards modification, interface definition, and vendor compliance testing flagged as high risk in the IRS Software Audit Guidelines, and verify that clean-room specifications handed to Team B define external functional targets rather than excluded "detailed specifications".

Replace Retrospective Estimates With Contemporaneous Artifacts: Substantiate the ≥80% experimentation fraction using version-control commit logs, finite-element or algorithmic simulation files, prototype failure reports, and task-level timesheets rather than retrospective management percentage estimates disallowed in Little Sandy Coal and Phoenix Design Group.

body.text: Tax Accounting Interaction: IRC Section 174A Domestic Expensing Versus Section 174 Amortization
1. Statutory Currency Update: Public Law 119-21 Enactment of IRC Section 174A (July 4, 2025)

Under Section 13206 of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (TCJA, Pub. L. No. 115-97, enacted December 22, 2017), domestic and foreign research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025, were subject to mandatory capitalization and amortization (over 5 years for domestic research and 15 years for foreign research) under IRC § 174. However, Public Law 119-21 (Title VII, § 70302, 139 Stat. 72, 190, enacted July 4, 2025) overhauled this regime for amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024.

Under newly enacted 26 U.S.C. § 174A(a)–(b), taxpayers are once again permitted to currently deduct domestic research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred during the taxable year (defined as research or experimental expenditures other than those attributable to foreign research within the meaning of IRC § 41(d)(4)(F), and explicitly including domestic software development under IRC § 174A(b)(3)), notwithstanding IRC § 263. Alternatively, taxpayers may elect under IRC § 174A(c) (no later than the return filing due date, including extensions) to charge domestic R&E expenditures to a capital account and amortize them ratably over a period of not less than 60 months beginning with the month in which the taxpayer first realizes benefits from the expenditures. In coordination with IRC § 174A, Section 70302(b)(2)(B) of Pub. L. 119-21 amended IRC § 280C(c)(1)–(2) so that domestic R&E deductions or capitalized amounts are reduced by the Section 41(a) research credit unless the taxpayer timely elects the reduced credit under IRC § 280C(c)(2).

In addition, Section 70302(f) of Pub. L. 119-21 and IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-28 (2025-38 I.R.B., modifying Rev. Proc. 2025-23) establish two key transition mechanisms for 2022–2024 domestic R&E costs. First, under the small-business retroactive expensing election in Section 70302(f)(1), eligible small-business taxpayers (taxpayers other than tax shelters under IRC § 448(a)(3) that meet the IRC § 448(c) gross-receipts test for their first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024) may elect by July 6, 2026 (extended from Saturday, July 4, 2026, under IRC § 7503) via amended returns or AARs to apply IRC § 174A and amended IRC § 280C retroactively to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, including making or revoking late IRC § 280C(c)(2) elections. Second, under Section 70302(f)(2), all taxpayers with unamortized domestic R&E amounts capitalized under TCJA Section 174 in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025, are provided automatic accounting-method-change procedures on a cut-off basis to adjust and accelerate recovery of remaining unamortized pre-2025 balances.

By contrast, Section 70302(b)(1) of Pub. L. 119-21 amended IRC § 174 so that it applies exclusively to foreign research or experimental expenditures (research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or U.S. territories/possessions under IRC § 41(d)(4)(F)). Foreign research expenditures remain categorically ineligible for the Section 41 credit under IRC § 41(d)(4)(F) and must continue to be capitalized and amortized ratably over a 15-year period beginning with the midpoint of the taxable year in which paid or incurred under amended IRC § 174 (with IRC § 174(d) barring immediate deduction upon disposition, retirement, or abandonment of foreign R&E property after May 12, 2025).
2. Substantive R&E Scope Under 26 CFR Section 1.174-2(a)(1) and (a)(6)

Even apart from the restoration of current domestic expensing under IRC § 174A, pure reverse engineering conducted merely to clone an existing product or gather competitive intelligence generally falls outside Section 174 and Section 174A altogether. Under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1), § 1.174-2(a)(6)(i)–(vi), and the IRS ATG, expenditures constitute R&E costs only when incurred in the experimental or laboratory sense to eliminate technical uncertainty regarding capability, method, or appropriate design—expressly excluding routine quality control testing, efficiency surveys, management or consumer surveys, and "the acquisition of another's patent, model, production or process". Accordingly, pure domestic teardown costs lacking design uncertainty are governed by general business-deduction or capital-expenditure provisions (IRC §§ 162 and 263) rather than IRC § 174A, whereas mandatory 15-year capitalization exposure under amended IRC § 174 applies specifically where foreign investigative R&E satisfies 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1) uncertainty (or where foreign software development is incurred) while failing Section 41 credit eligibility.
